name: Owens v. Haas
court: Second Circuit (from the Eastern District of New York)
topic: County liability under section 1983 for failure to train and supervise correctional officers after a beating in a county jail; pleading and discovery after Monell; hands and feet
summary: A federal prisoner housed under contract in the Nassau County Jail refused to leave his cell to sign for a warrant, and about seven officers beat him severely. The district court dismissed his section 1983 claim against the county because no official policy or pattern had been pleaded. The Second Circuit reversed, holding that a county may be liable if its failure to supervise or lack of a proper training program was so severe as to amount to gross negligence or deliberate indifference, that a single brutal incident may be enough to suggest the causal link, and that the prisoner should have limited discovery and a chance to amend. It is taught as the first appellate statement, a year after Monell, that a jail's failure to train its officers can be the county's own wrong.
coverage: The opinion was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F2/601/601.F2d.1242.79-7043.825.html. The header carries 601 F.2d 1242, No. 825, Docket 79-7043, which is how the citation was confirmed. The archive text is paragraph numbered; no reporter page pin cites are given.

Rymer v. Davis, 754 F.2d 198 (6th Cir. 1985), read for this project, cites the denial of certiorari in Owens as 444 U.S. 980 (1979). That citation was not independently verified from a Supreme Court source.

The district court's opinion at 456 F.Supp. 1009 and the hearing before Judge Bartels were not read. The incident is described only as the Second Circuit recited the plaintiff's account and the hearing testimony it mentioned.
This was a ruling on the pleadings. No court found the county liable. What happened on remand was not checked.

The opinion also addressed section 1985 and a third-party beneficiary contract claim under the federal-county prisoner housing contract. Those holdings are summarized briefly because they are not the reason the case is taught.
facts:
The facts below are the plaintiff's allegations and the testimony the Second Circuit referred to. The case was decided on the pleadings, so nothing was found to be true.

Dewitt Owens was a federal prisoner cooperating with the government. For his safety he was transferred in August 1976 to the Nassau County Jail in Hicksville, New York, under a contract between the Bureau of Prisons and Nassau County authorized by 18 U.S.C. section 4002.

On October 27, 1976, according to Owens, a guard woke him and told him to report downstairs to acknowledge the lodging of a warrant against him. Owens refused, protesting that he had already signed for a warrant, and apparently believed he did not have to sign. The guard left. Later First Class Corrections Officer Haas came to the cell. Owens again refused to leave, the two argued, and Haas told him to pack his things because he was going to a more secure locked cell on another floor. Insults were exchanged and Haas left.

Fifteen or twenty minutes later several officers returned and ordered Owens out. After an argument he stepped out of the cell. About seven guards were present. Owens was grabbed and beaten severely, suffering lacerations, bruises and lasting impairments that caused blackouts.

Shortly afterward Owens appeared before a federal district judge for sentencing in an unrelated case. The judge noticed his injuries, questioned him, and ordered a hearing at which Owens and several jail officials testified. At that hearing Officer Haas mentioned that one of the officers involved, Officer Allen, was fairly new on the job, and described his philosophy that a show of force by several officers is a good way to control an inmate who refuses an order.

Owens sued in April 1977 under sections 1983 and 1985 and for breach of contract as a third-party beneficiary of the federal-county contract. When he filed, Monroe v. Pape still barred suits against municipalities; Monell was decided in 1978 while the case was pending. The district court granted judgment on the pleadings to the county, reading Monell to require that the beating be part of an official policy or custom or one of a series of incidents known to the county, and also rejected the contract claims. The court entered judgment for the county under Rule 54(b), and Owens appealed.
holding:
Reversed and remanded.

Section 1983. The district court read Monell too narrowly. The court agreed that a mere failure by the county to supervise its employees would not be enough, citing Rizzo v. Goode. But the county could be held liable if the failure to supervise or the lack of a proper training program was so severe as to reach the level of gross negligence or deliberate indifference to the deprivation of the plaintiff's constitutional rights. This concept does not hold the county at fault for the actions of its employees on a respondeat superior basis; it holds the county liable for its own actions which result in deprivation of constitutional rights.

The court found some indication that such a claim could be raised. From Haas's testimony that Officer Allen was fairly new and that a show of force is a good way to control an inmate, it could be inferred that an officer new to the job might not be properly prepared and that a show of force might get out of hand in the absence of proper training. The brutal and premeditated nature of the beating and the number and rank of officers involved warranted limited discovery so the plaintiff could attempt to substantiate a claim of deliberate indifference by the county to the violence of prison officials, stemming from a failure to train the guards in an adequate manner.

On the single incident problem, the court held that while some causal link must be shown between the county's failure to train and the violation, a single brutal incident such as this may be sufficient to suggest that link. Quoting Leite v. City of Providence, it said citizens need not endure a pattern of past misconduct before suing, and that a municipality is fairly considered to have actual or imputed knowledge of the almost inevitable consequences of nonexistent or grossly inadequate training and supervision. The court repeated that the failure to train or supervise must be so grossly negligent as to constitute deliberate indifference, and said the circumstances of this severe beating suggested official acquiescence on some level. The remedy was limited discovery and leave to amend, balancing the concern about groundless suits against municipalities with the rule that civil rights actions should not be dismissed at the pleading stage unless the plaintiff could not recover under any provable facts.

Section 1985. Assuming a county is a person under section 1985 as under section 1983, a conspiracy claim would lie if the amended complaint alleged an official custom or policy implicating the county itself.

Contract claims. No private right of action is implied under 18 U.S.C. section 4002. But federal law governs the federal-county contract, New York law may be consulted, and the Bureau of Prisons policy statement incorporated into the contract, which required a secure, humane and orderly environment and only the minimum force required to gain control, suggested Owens might be an intended beneficiary able to sue on it. That claim was remanded.
notDecided:
Whether Nassau County was liable, or whether its training was inadequate. The court held only that the plaintiff should have discovery and a chance to amend.

Whether the beating happened as alleged. The case was decided on the pleadings.

The individual officers' liability. Only the judgment for the county was on appeal.

Whether a single incident alone can establish municipal liability. The court said a single brutal incident may be sufficient to suggest the causal link, and still required proof that the failure to train was grossly negligent to the point of deliberate indifference. Later Supreme Court decisions, including Oklahoma City v. Tuttle and City of Canton v. Harris, addressed this question and should be taught alongside Owens.

Whether Owens was in fact a third-party beneficiary, which was remanded.
inPractice:
Owens is a custody case. A refusal to leave a cell for a routine administrative task became a cell extraction by about seven officers and a beating a federal judge noticed from the bench. The court's path to the county ran through two pieces of testimony: that one officer was fairly new, and that the senior officer believed a show of force is a good way to control an inmate who refuses an order.

For correctional officers: the number of staff present is not a use of force plan. The court inferred that a show of force might get out of hand without proper training. Numbers without a trained method, assigned roles and supervisory control is what the court saw.

For supervisors: a newly hired officer on an extraction team is a training question before it is a discipline question. The court treated the new officer's presence as a reason to let the plaintiff look into the county's training.

For the agency: the court said deliberate indifference holds the county liable for its own actions. The question in discovery would be what training the jail gave its officers in controlling a non-compliant inmate, and the answer would have to come from records.

For contract facilities: the Bureau of Prisons policy statement incorporated into the housing contract required only the minimum force required to gain control of the situation and to prevent injury. The court read that language as possibly creating rights the prisoner could enforce.
trainIt:
Teach the trigger: a refusal to comply with a low-stakes order. Scenario training for cell extractions and escorts should start there, with verbal resolution, time, and a supervisor's decision, before any team enters.

Train the team, not just the individuals. Owens turned on the idea that several officers acting without a trained plan might get out of hand. Teach assigned roles, a single leader, a planned level of force, and a stop point. Document who has completed the training before assigning them to a team.

Address new officers specifically. The only training-related facts the court mentioned were that one officer was fairly new and that the senior officer believed in a show of force. A field training record that shows what a new officer has been taught about use of force in custody is the agency's answer to the inference the court drew.

Teach the standard as the court stated it: the failure to train or supervise must be so grossly negligent as to constitute deliberate indifference, and it is the county's own fault, not vicarious liability. Then teach that Canton later fixed deliberate indifference as the standard and that the single incident question was narrowed by Tuttle.

Teach the posture: this opinion reversed a dismissal on the pleadings and allowed limited discovery. It did not find the county liable or find the training inadequate. Its value is the court's reasoning about why a jail's training is the county's responsibility.
caution: The opinion was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org archive, which is paragraph numbered, so no page pin cites are given. The decision is a 1979 pleading-stage ruling; it found no facts and imposed no liability. Its gross negligence language predates City of Canton v. Harris, which settled deliberate indifference as the standard, and its single incident reasoning predates Oklahoma City v. Tuttle. The certiorari denial citation is as reported in Rymer v. Davis and was not independently verified.

applications.title: A show of force is not a plan
applications.body: The senior officer's philosophy that several officers present is a good way to control a refusing inmate was, in the court's view, evidence that a show of force might get out of hand without proper training. Teams need trained roles and a controlled method.

applications.title: New officers on extraction teams raise a training question
applications.body: The court cited testimony that one officer was fairly new as a reason to allow discovery into the county's training. Field training records for new custody staff answer that question.

applications.title: The county's liability is for its own conduct
applications.body: The court was explicit that deliberate indifference liability is not respondeat superior. It is the agency's own failure to train or supervise, so the agency's own records are the proof either way.

applications.title: Contract language about force can matter
applications.body: The federal housing contract required only the minimum force required to gain control and to prevent injury. The court held the prisoner might be able to enforce it as a third-party beneficiary. Know what your facility's contracts promise.

applications.title: Teach the posture
applications.body: Owens reversed a dismissal and allowed limited discovery. It is not a finding of liability. Teach it with Hays, Rymer and Canton to show how the standard developed.

quiz.q: What did the Second Circuit decide in Owens v. Haas?
options: It found Nassau County liable for failing to train its correctional officers
It reversed the dismissal of the section 1983 claim against the county and allowed limited discovery and amendment so the plaintiff could try to show deliberate indifference in training
It held that counties can never be liable for jail beatings
It affirmed because only a single incident was alleged
quiz.teach: This was a pleading-stage decision. The court held the district court read Monell too narrowly and sent the case back for discovery. No liability was found.

quiz.q: What testimony did the court point to as suggesting a possible failure to train claim?
options: That the jail had no written use of force policy
That one officer involved was fairly new on the job and the senior officer believed a show of force is a good way to control an inmate who refuses an order
That the officers had been disciplined before
That the warden had ignored a prior lawsuit
quiz.teach: The court inferred that a new officer might not be properly prepared and that a show of force might get out of hand without proper training. It treated the brutality and the number of officers as warranting discovery.

quiz.q: What standard did the court say the failure to train or supervise must meet?
options: So grossly negligent as to constitute deliberate indifference, as the county's own fault rather than respondeat superior
Intent to injure the particular prisoner
quiz.teach: The court distinguished a mere failure to supervise, which is not enough, from a failure so severe it amounts to gross negligence or deliberate indifference. Canton later settled on deliberate indifference.
